An important tip with basil: Do not add it when you are still cooking on anything other than low. Higher heat destroys the taste of the basil. As for onions and garlic, for me, it depends on what I am cooking. If you are in it for the taste of the meat itself (like a steak), they go in last. There are a lot of meats that are more like blank slates (like chicken) that need to absorb the flavors for the best outcome. As for most other herbs, those are best rubbed in long before you start cooking in most things (such as ribs, lamb, chicken, most non steak cuts of beef.) Don't mess with steaks with too much additives though. The best steak is the one that is flavored with salt (and maybe some pepper.) Just keep in mind your goals. A juicy steak is juicy because of melted fat, not water. You lose flavor to water being present. I like to use coarse salt on a steak, with paper towels on top and beneath it. The salt pulls out water and starts to denature the proteins that make it tough. When you are ready to cook it, you brush of most of the salt (which is easy because it is coarse,) then cook it according to steak type. Just think about the meat you are cooking and try to accentuate the best part of it.

I remember seeing an episode of one of Alton Brown's shows and he mentioned that if you're salting a steak, to either salt it and let it sit for 5-10 minutes before hitting the pan. No longer than that because of protein denaturing. But he also noticed that if you let it sit in the fridge for 24 hrs, it actually makes the steak better. I forget why this is and can't find the source, but I distinctly remember him saying "No more than 10 minutes unless you can leave it over night."

It really depends on the flavor profile you're trying to build. I personally enjoy very-toasted garlic so I actually start my garlic before throwing onions in to brown. Let the garlic sit there until they JUST start developing some brown on them and then throw the onions in. So by the time the onions are ready and you add your protein, the garlic is a nice dark-brown or black.
